text:
The American aviation industry has a target: produce 3 billion gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually by 2030.

It’s an ambitious number, and it’s central to the industry’s plans for reducing its carbon footprint without waiting for a new generation of aircraft.

A new study from Washington State University (WSU) takes a hard look at whether the US can actually get there.

The short answer is probably not – but the longer answer is more instructive than the headline.

An industry that won’t explode overnight

The research offers one of the most detailed assessments yet of the U.S. sustainable aviation fuel industry.

The experts found that even in the most optimistic scenario, domestic production is likely to reach around 2.1 billion gallons per year by 2030.

Under less favorable conditions, the actual figure could be considerably lower.

“We wanted to take a very pragmatic look at where we really are,” said study lead author Kristin Brandt from WSU.

“There are people saying this industry is going to explode overnight and others saying nothing will happen at all. The reality is somewhere in between.”

Why sustainable aviation fuel matters

Commercial aircraft are genuinely difficult to decarbonize. Unlike cars, they can’t be electrified in any practical near-term sense – the energy density of batteries simply isn’t there yet for long-haul flights.

Replacing the world’s fleet of aircraft would take decades. Replacing the global fuelling infrastructure that supports them would take even longer.

Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) sidesteps those problems by working with what already exists. It can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used in current aircraft without modification.

Depending on how it’s produced, it can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by around 80% compared to conventional petroleum-based jet fuel.

Current production relies heavily on renewable or waste-based fats and oils such as used cooking oil, animal fats, or vegetable oils.

That combination – large emissions reductions, no need to change planes or airports – makes SAF one of the most practical near-term tools aviation has for reducing its climate impact.

Projects that are not operational

The WSU team did something that sounds straightforward but rarely gets done rigorously: they looked at how many announced fuel projects actually become operational.

They analyzed publicly announced US renewable fuel projects stretching back more than two decades, tracking whether facilities got built, how long construction took, and whether production targets were met.

The pattern they found was consistent. About half of all announced projects never become operational.

Many projects are delayed, some are scaled back, and a few are cancelled outright.

Ambitious timelines announced at press conferences frequently don’t survive contact with permitting processes, financing conditions, and supply chain realities.

The gap between hope and reality

To account for this, the researchers developed what they call an “implementation ratio” – an estimate of how many announced facilities will actually get built, based on historical performance.

It’s a useful corrective to the industry’s natural tendency toward optimism.

“Announcements are not the same thing as fuel,” Brandt said. “People announce giant facilities with aggressive timelines all the time, but historically many projects get delayed, scaled back or never move forward.”

The cooking oil problem

One of the more unexpected findings involves feedstock – the raw materials from which SAF is produced.

The dominant production technology through 2030 is expected to be a process called hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids, or HEFA. This relies primarily on fats, oils, and greases, including used cooking oil and animal fats.

The problem is supply. Used cooking oil sounds like an abundant waste product – restaurants and food manufacturers generate it constantly.

But global demand for it, from SAF producers and other biodiesel manufacturers, has grown faster than supply..

“There’s actually a global shortage of used cooking oil,” Brandt said. “It sounds ridiculous, but it’s true.”

This matters because it caps how much HEFA-based SAF can be produced regardless of how many facilities get built. A plant without feedstock doesn’t make fuel.

Renewable diesel is a roadblock

There’s another obstacle that’s less about resources and more about economics.

Producers of renewable fats and oils face a choice: turn their feedstock into SAF, or turn it into renewable diesel for cars and trucks.

Under current US policies and market conditions, renewable diesel is often more profitable.

That creates a financial incentive to divert feedstock away from aviation fuel, limiting how much SAF actually gets produced even when the raw materials are available.

Fixing this requires either changing the relative economics – through policy adjustments, tax incentives, or mandates – or creating enough demand certainty that SAF becomes the more attractive option for producers.

How to hit the target

The researchers lay out clearly what would need to happen for the US to close the gap between projected production and the 2030 target.

First, sustained policy support and continued industry investment are both essential.

In addition, faster project completion rates, and solutions to the feedstock constraints that are already limiting growth are also needed to solve the current problems.

“Bringing about societal changes in energy systems are enormous transitions,” said co-author Michael Wolcott from WSU. “It will take years and multiple disciplines to realize progress.”

A realistic look at the barriers

Aviation is also global in a way that makes unilateral national solutions incomplete. Airlines fly international routes regardless of where their planes are registered.

If global standards tighten – as they are expected to – carriers operating internationally will need to meet those standards regardless of domestic policy differences.

“This is something the industry is going to have to work through together,” Brandt said.

The 2030 target probably won’t be met. But the industry is moving, the technology works, and the constraints are at least identifiable.

“If we want to hit these goals, we need to be honest about the barriers and realistic about what it will take to overcome them,” Brandt concluded.

The study is published in the journal Biomass and Bioenergy.

text:
Japan’s two largest airlines are calling for a nationwide effort to accelerate the use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), warning that the industry faces a looming crisis if action is not taken soon.

All Nippon Airways (ANA) and Japan Airlines released the second edition of their joint report on SAF on May 27, 2026.

Titled “Toward Net Zero CO2 Emissions from Air Transport in 2050,” the report outlines the current state of sustainable fuel adoption in Japan and what it will take to meet the aviation industry’s climate goals.

A small slice of the fuel mix

SAF is considered essential for reducing carbon emissions from flying, but the report notes that it made up just 0.6% of global aviation fuel consumption as of 2025. Without a significant increase in production and cost reductions over the next five years, the aviation industry risks falling short of its emissions targets, with potential ripple effects across the economy.

Japan’s aviation sector generates an estimated JPY 17 trillion (US $110 billion) in annual economic activity and plays a critical role in connecting regional communities and remote islands that depend on air service. The country is also aiming to attract 60 million inbound visitors, a goal that depends on a stable and sustainable fuel supply.

A Japanese approach

The report proposes what it calls a “Japanese Model,” an approach that balances the pace of SAF regulations with the country’s actual domestic production capacity. The idea is to avoid supply shortages and excessive costs while supporting long-term growth.

ANA and JAL are also promoting what they describe as a “Co-creation Model,” in which the high costs of SAF adoption are shared across society rather than borne by airlines alone. Through corporate programs, both carriers are helping business customers reduce their own emissions tied to air travel.

Rivals working together

Despite being competitors, ANA and JAL say they are working together as the “two wings” of Japan’s aviation sector to address a challenge that goes beyond any single company.

Juichi Hirasawa, President and CEO of ANA, said the global SAF landscape is severe and any delay in securing fuel represents a direct threat to Japan’s economic security.

“We strongly call for an effective, society-wide framework to maintain Japan’s aviation infrastructure and hand over sustainable skies to the next generation,” Hirasawa said.

Mitsuko Tottori, President and Group CEO of JAL, echoed the sentiment, saying that while scaling SAF presents major challenges, the airline remains committed to pioneering a sustainable future.

“Moving forward together with All Nippon Airways, and hand in hand with our customers and all stakeholders, we will face these difficulties to ensure a vibrant future of movement is securely passed to the next generation,” Tottori said.

The report follows the first joint SAF report released by the two airlines in October 2021.

text:
Loganair has entered a 15-year sustainable aviation fuel supply agreement with ClimaHtech Green Flight to secure long-term access to cleaner fuel and reduce exposure to rising compliance costs from the UK government’s SAF mandate.

Loganair expects to receive fuel deliveries under the agreement starting in 2029.

The deal aims to provide price certainty and shield the airline from regulatory and market volatility as the aviation sector faces pressure to decarbonize. Financial terms and fuel volume tied to the agreement have not been disclosed.

Through this arrangement, ClimaHtech Green Flight will supply fuel produced via both BioSAF and eSAF pathways. BioSAF refers to SAF produced from biological sources, such as plants or waste, while eSAF refers to SAF produced using renewable energy and captured carbon. These methods utilize a combination of biomass feedstocks, renewable electricity, and advanced synthetic fuel technologies to reduce lifecycle emissions compared to conventional jet fuel.

The partnership will develop production infrastructure across pivotal areas of Loganair’s operating network, including the Scottish Highlands and Islands, regional UK routes, and Northern Ireland. By locating production facilities near the point of use, the companies aim to cut transportation costs and reduce exposure to broader global supply chain disruptions.

The regional production strategy also aligns with growing industry interest in decentralized energy systems that can better support local aviation demand.

ClimaHtech Green Flight is advancing project development, including regulatory approvals and site selection. The company says its electrically driven platform operates with intermittent renewable energy and waste biomass feedstocks, lowering costs and boosting flexibility.

The agreement comes as European airlines seek long-term sustainable aviation fuel partnerships ahead of stricter emissions rules and growing pressure to reduce air travel’s environmental impact.

“As the UK’s largest regional airline, Loganair plays a vital role in connecting communities across the UK, particularly in areas where aviation is a lifeline rather than a luxury,” said Luke Farajallah, chief executive of Loganair. “Decarbonizing regional aviation is therefore both a responsibility and a practical challenge. This long-term agreement with ClimaHtech Green Flight is an important step in securing access to Sustainable Aviation Fuel that is produced closer to where we operate, supports UK supply chains, and reflects our commitment to lowering our carbon footprint.”

Mel Courtney, chief executive of ClimaHtech Green Flight, said the deal “shows Loganair’s confidence in our SAF pathways and our regional SAF production model.”

“The ClimaHtech platform handles intermittent renewable power, allowing direct renewable energy connections. Efficient energy and biomass use bring scalable, resilient SAF deployment,” he said.
